basis: Original PBSC Cohort Zero agenda; all lesson explanations are optional additional instructional material, not official presentation transcripts.

lessons.title: Welcome and Program Introduction
lessons.overview: Understand the five-day journey, the distinction between concepts and measured evidence, and how to make a useful workshop record.

concepts.heading: What the workshop covers
concepts.text: The agenda moves from qubit fundamentals and quantum circuits to communications and cryptography, technician skills, Python, and experiments with classical waves. Each block introduces a different skill; none by itself certifies proficiency with quantum hardware.

concepts.heading: Three kinds of evidence
concepts.text: A mathematical prediction is a consequence of assumptions; a software simulation approximates a model; a laboratory measurement is obtained from an instrument with calibration and uncertainty. Label them separately so an instructor can reproduce the result.

concepts.heading: Safe and productive participation
concepts.text: Record questions, apparatus settings, screenshots, units, and conclusions. Follow instructor supervision and manufacturer guidance when working with lasers, electronics, fiber optics, or power supplies. Do not infer actual quantum behavior from a classical analogy alone.

worked.title: A good workshop entry
steps: Write the question: What is the predicted probability of measuring 0 after a Hadamard gate on |0⟩?
State the model: ideal single qubit, no noise, Z-basis measurement.
State the prediction: P(0) = 1/2.
Record whether the evidence came from a simulator or actual quantum device.
worked.result: A reproducible learning record separates prediction, method, observation, and conclusion.

practice.question: Why must a graph have an evidence label?
practice.answer: Because an ideal simulator plot, a sampled measurement, and a physical instrument trace have different limitations.

lessons.misconception: A simulation is not automatically an experimental measurement.

lessons.title: Introduction to Quantum Computing and Qubits
lessons.overview: Learn how quantum information differs from a classical bit and how amplitudes lead to measurement probabilities.

concepts.heading: Classical bits and qubits
concepts.text: A classical bit stores 0 or 1. A pure qubit has a state |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩, where α and β are complex amplitudes and |α|² + |β|² = 1. The complex phase between amplitudes can matter to later operations.

concepts.heading: Measurement and probabilities
concepts.text: A single ideal Z-basis measurement yields only 0 or 1, with probabilities P(0)=|α|² and P(1)=|β|². Repeating a preparation many times produces classical counts; it does not reveal both amplitudes from one measurement.

concepts.heading: Why quantum gates matter
concepts.text: Gates act on amplitudes while the state is coherent. Interference of probability amplitudes can change later outcome probabilities. The usefulness of a circuit depends on the algorithm, not just on having many possible states.

worked.title: Normalize a state
steps: Start with amplitudes α=3/5 and β=4i/5.
Compute |α|² = 9/25 and |β|² = 16/25.
Add: 9/25 + 16/25 = 1, so the state is normalized.
Predict Z measurement: P(0)=36%; P(1)=64%.

practice.question: A state has amplitudes 1/√2 and i/√2. What is P(1)?

lessons.misconception: A qubit does not produce a readable continuous value during one Z measurement.

lessons.title: Introduction to Bloch Sphere and gates
lessons.overview: Connect pure single-qubit states to geometric directions and use gates to predict state changes.

concepts.heading: Reading the sphere
concepts.text: The north pole is |0⟩ and the south pole is |1⟩. The +X direction is |+⟩=(|0⟩+|1⟩)/√2; −X is |−⟩=(|0⟩−|1⟩)/√2. The ±Y states differ by the sign of an imaginary phase. These are mathematical state directions, not the physical location of a particle.

concepts.heading: Angles and measurement
concepts.text: For a pure state cos(θ/2)|0⟩ + exp(iφ)sin(θ/2)|1⟩, the Bloch vector is (sinθ cosφ, sinθ sinφ, cosθ). In Z, P(0)=(1+z)/2. Changing φ at fixed θ can change X/Y outcomes without changing Z probabilities.

concepts.heading: Gate transformations
concepts.text: X flips |0⟩ and |1⟩. H maps |0⟩ to |+⟩ and turns phase information into measurable outcomes. Z changes the sign of |1⟩ relative to |0⟩: Z|+⟩=|−⟩. Gates preserve normalization in an ideal closed system.

worked.title: Predict the sequence H → Z → H
steps: Prepare |0⟩: P(0)=1 in Z.
Apply H: state becomes |+⟩; Z measurement would be 50/50.
Apply Z: state becomes |−⟩; Z probabilities remain 50/50.
Apply H: state becomes |1⟩; Z measurement now gives 1 with certainty.
worked.result: HZH acts like X on |0⟩. The intervening phase becomes observable after the last H.

practice.question: Why is Z|+⟩ different from |+⟩ even though both are 50/50 in Z?
practice.answer: They have different relative phase and are perfectly distinguishable in the X basis.

lessons.misconception: Moving a vector on the Bloch sphere is a state transformation, not a particle orbit.

lessons.title: Introduction to IBM Qiskit
lessons.overview: Construct a single-qubit circuit with Qiskit, explain each line, and distinguish circuit construction from executing it on hardware.

concepts.heading: Circuit representation
concepts.text: Qiskit uses QuantumCircuit to define qubit registers, classical results, gate operations, and measurements. A circuit is a program description; printing its diagram does not execute it on quantum hardware.

concepts.heading: Create, modify, and inspect
concepts.text: Start with one qubit and one classical bit. Apply H on qubit 0 to create |+⟩, then measure qubit 0 into classical bit 0. Change H to X and predict which Z outcome should become certain.

concepts.heading: Sampling and hardware
concepts.text: On an ideal simulator, repeated shots of H|0⟩ approach a 50/50 count of outcomes. Actual hardware may differ because of noise and readout errors. Running on IBM Quantum hardware requires supported software, access, and the user's own authorized account.

worked.title: Explain a Qiskit starter
steps: from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
qc = QuantumCircuit(1, 1)  # one qubit and one classical bit
qc.h(0)  # create equal Z-basis probabilities
qc.measure(0, 0)  # record 0 or 1 in the classical bit
print(qc.draw())  # draw the circuit; does not execute it
worked.result: The circuit predicts 50/50 Z outcomes on ideal repeated execution; printing is only a diagram.

practice.question: Change qc.h(0) to qc.x(0). What ideal outcome is expected?
practice.answer: X|0⟩=|1⟩, so every ideal Z measurement returns 1.

lessons.misconception: Calling measure or draw is not the same as submitting a job to real quantum hardware.

lessons.title: Review of previous day
lessons.overview: Review Monday's core predictions before connecting quantum behavior to networks.

concepts.heading: Recall the models
concepts.text: A qubit uses complex amplitudes, measurement returns a classical result, and relative phase changes some basis probabilities. Check that |α|²+|β|²=1.

concepts.heading: Read the Bloch sphere
concepts.text: Describe where |0⟩, |1⟩, |+⟩, and |−⟩ are on the sphere; distinguish Z and X measurement.

concepts.heading: Explain a circuit
concepts.text: For H then Z then H on |0⟩, reason through each state before calculating the final outcome.

worked.title: One-minute whiteboard check
steps: Write |0⟩.
Apply H to get |+⟩.
Apply Z to get |−⟩.
Apply H to get |1⟩.
worked.result: A final ideal Z measurement gives 1 with probability 1.

practice.question: What does qc.draw() do?
practice.answer: It shows the circuit; it does not run an experiment.

lessons.misconception: A diagram cannot establish hardware performance.

lessons.title: Intro to Computer Networking and Encryption
lessons.overview: Understand how network layers, secret keys, public keys, and authentication protect data.

concepts.heading: The communication path
concepts.text: A sender creates data, a transport carries packets, and a receiver interprets them. Routers and other intermediaries may carry traffic. Protecting data therefore requires security properties beyond a reliable link.

concepts.heading: Symmetric versus public-key cryptography
concepts.text: Symmetric encryption uses a shared secret key to encrypt and decrypt (for example, AES). Public-key methods help establish secrets or verify signatures. A hash produces a digest, but hashing alone is not encryption.

concepts.heading: Security goals and quantum risk
concepts.text: Confidentiality keeps data secret; integrity detects changes; authentication checks identity. TLS commonly combines an authenticated key exchange with efficient symmetric encryption. Large-scale fault-tolerant quantum computers threaten widely deployed RSA and elliptic-curve public-key schemes; this motivates migration to PQC.

worked.title: Trace a secure connection
steps: A browser connects to a server and receives an authenticated certificate chain.
A key-establishment process derives secrets; an authenticated handshake prevents a simple impostor from taking over.
Traffic is protected with symmetric authenticated encryption.
The receiver verifies integrity/authenticity and recovers the plaintext.
worked.result: Encryption and authentication solve different problems and are used together.

practice.question: If a message is encrypted but the sender is not authenticated, what risk remains?
practice.answer: An attacker could impersonate a party or establish a different encrypted session; encryption alone does not prove identity.

lessons.misconception: A hash is not a reversible cipher and cannot replace authentication by itself.

lessons.title: Energy Polarization
lessons.overview: Explore polarization as a transverse-wave property and connect polarizer angles to measured optical intensity.

concepts.heading: Electric field direction
concepts.text: In a plane electromagnetic wave, the electric and magnetic fields are transverse to the propagation direction. Linear polarization describes the electric field's oscillation direction in the plane perpendicular to propagation.

concepts.heading: Malus's law
concepts.text: For ideal linearly polarized light entering an ideal analyzer at relative angle θ, transmitted intensity is I=I₀cos²θ. At 0°, transmission is 100%; at 60°, 25%; at 90°, ideally 0. Real optics have losses and finite extinction.

concepts.heading: Quantum interpretation
concepts.text: Individual photon polarization can encode qubit states. Its measurement probabilities follow related trigonometric dependence, but classical beam intensity and single-photon detection statistics are different kinds of evidence.

worked.title: Work a polarizer problem
steps: Start with linearly polarized light of intensity I₀=8 mW/cm².
Rotate a second ideal polarizer by 60°.
Calculate cos²60°=(1/2)²=1/4.
Therefore I=8×1/4=2 mW/cm².
worked.result: The ideal analyzer transmits 25% of the incoming polarized intensity.

practice.question: What happens for crossed ideal polarizers at 90°?
practice.answer: cos²90°=0; ideal transmitted intensity is zero, but real devices may leak light.

lessons.misconception: Polarization direction is not the same as optical propagation direction; never view laser beams directly.

lessons.title: Quantum Key Distribution
lessons.overview: Understand the BB84 prepare–measure–sift logic and the need for authenticated classical discussion.

concepts.heading: The BB84 idea
concepts.text: Alice encodes randomly selected bits in one of two bases, such as Z and X. Bob independently chooses a measurement basis. Afterward they publicly compare only the bases, not their secret bit values; positions with different bases are discarded.

concepts.heading: Why errors matter
concepts.text: If Bob matches Alice's basis and there is no noise or eavesdropping, the ideal bit agrees. An intercept–resend eavesdropper who guesses a random basis can cause detectable errors in the sifted bits. The ideal random-basis intercept–resend model gives about 25% sifted error, not a universal QKD security threshold.

concepts.heading: What is missing from the toy demo
concepts.text: A complete QKD system requires an authenticated classical channel, parameter estimation, error correction, privacy amplification, trusted equipment assumptions, and implementation security. QKD distributes key material; it does not itself encrypt application messages.

worked.title: Sift eight illustrative trials
steps: Alice bases: Z X Z X Z X Z X.
Bob bases: Z Z Z X X X Z Z.
Keep positions 1, 3, 4, 6, and 7 where the bases agree.
Discard positions 2, 5, and 8, then test a sample of the retained bits for errors.
worked.result: Five of eight positions are retained in this illustrative sequence; random long runs retain about half on average.

practice.question: Why must Alice and Bob authenticate their classical discussion?
practice.answer: Without authentication an attacker could impersonate participants and perform a man-in-the-middle attack.

lessons.misconception: Matching bases alone does not prove a secure key was produced.

lessons.title: Review of previous day
lessons.overview: Review Tuesday's networking, polarization, and BB84 foundations.

concepts.heading: Network security recap
concepts.text: Distinguish confidentiality, integrity, and authentication. A secret key and an authenticated identity do different jobs.

concepts.heading: Polarization recap
concepts.text: Recall Malus's law and interpret 0°, 60°, and 90° analyzer angles under ideal assumptions.

concepts.heading: QKD recap
concepts.text: Describe basis choices, sifting, and why an authenticated public discussion is still required.

worked.title: Mini-check: angle and intensity
steps: An ideal analyzer is 60° from the incident linear polarization.
Calculate cos²60°=1/4.
Predict one-quarter of the incident polarized intensity.
Label whether the observation is classical intensity or photon counts.

practice.question: Does BB84 create an already encrypted message?
practice.answer: No. It aims to establish shared key material, which can then be used by encryption.

lessons.misconception: Quantum key distribution and post-quantum algorithms are different technologies.

lessons.title: Introduction to Post Quantum Cryptology
lessons.overview: Learn what post-quantum cryptography protects, which current NIST standards apply, and how it differs from QKD.

concepts.heading: The threat model
concepts.text: Shor's algorithm on sufficiently capable fault-tolerant quantum computers threatens common integer-factorization and discrete-log public-key systems such as RSA and elliptic-curve schemes. Current risk also includes collecting encrypted traffic today for decryption later.

concepts.heading: Standards to recognize
concepts.text: NIST FIPS 203 defines ML-KEM for establishing a shared secret. FIPS 204 defines ML-DSA digital signatures. FIPS 205 defines SLH-DSA hash-based digital signatures. ML-KEM is a key-encapsulation mechanism, not a general replacement for AES data encryption.

concepts.heading: PQC versus QKD
concepts.text: PQC runs as algorithms on conventional computing and network infrastructure. QKD uses physical quantum states and specialized communication equipment; both require system-level design and authentication.

worked.title: Choose the correct tool
steps: Problem A: two systems need to establish a shared session secret over a network.
Use a suitable KEM such as ML-KEM in an approved protocol, then authenticated symmetric encryption for traffic.
Problem B: a software publisher must sign an update.
Choose an appropriate digital-signature scheme such as ML-DSA and verify the publisher's identity.
worked.result: Key establishment and digital signatures protect different security requirements.

practice.question: Is ML-KEM the same thing as a digital signature?
practice.answer: No. ML-KEM establishes key material; ML-DSA and SLH-DSA are digital signature standards.

lessons.misconception: Quantum-resistant does not mean invulnerable; correct implementations and migration planning matter.

lessons.title: Post Quantum Cryptology Implementation
lessons.overview: Plan a practical post-quantum migration without treating an algorithm name as a complete secure deployment.

concepts.heading: Discover dependencies
concepts.text: Inventory TLS endpoints, PKI certificates, VPNs, firmware signing, HSMs, third-party libraries, embedded devices, and long-lived encrypted archives. Note ownership, supported algorithms, upgrade paths, and data retention periods.

concepts.heading: Choose supported protocols
concepts.text: Select vetted implementations following standards and vendor guidance. Understand key encapsulation versus signatures, certificate-chain compatibility, message sizes, latency, entropy requirements, authentication, and failure behavior.

concepts.heading: Pilot, measure, and roll out
concepts.text: Test on a nonproduction environment with representative clients, gateways, and devices. Record handshake success rates, bandwidth, processor cost, failed connections, certificate handling, version rollback, and audit logs. Move gradually with monitoring and rollback procedures.

worked.title: A small migration exercise
steps: Inventory: website TLS termination, mobile client, VPN, and update-signing server.
Classify data sensitivity and how long recordings must remain confidential.
Select one pilot path; verify standards-based support across both endpoints.
Measure interoperability, timing, certificate behavior, and connection failure cases.
Document a staged rollout and rollback plan.
worked.result: A successful migration is an interoperable, monitored system—not merely a new library function.

practice.question: Why test the oldest client before rollout?
practice.answer: A newly configured server can break clients that lack algorithm or protocol support, even when its algorithm is sound.

lessons.misconception: Never implement production cryptography from scratch for a classroom demo.

lessons.title: Review of previous day
lessons.overview: Review PQC fundamentals and translate the security concepts into an engineering plan.

concepts.heading: What the acronyms do
concepts.text: ML-KEM supports establishing shared secrets; ML-DSA and SLH-DSA support digital signatures. Neither alone supplies a full authenticated application protocol.

concepts.heading: Implementation questions
concepts.text: Ask what needs protection, where vulnerable cryptography is used, which devices are constrained, how the solution is tested, and how problems will be reversed safely.

concepts.heading: Boundary check
concepts.text: Distinguish deployed production cryptography from illustrative pseudocode; avoid claiming a key exchange succeeded unless both peers and authentication were actually tested.

worked.title: Match requirements to standards
steps: A secure channel needs authenticated secret establishment.
A firmware update needs signer authentication and integrity.
Map the first need to protocol-level use of a KEM, and the second to a verified digital signature.
Plan interoperability and negative test cases before deployment.
worked.result: Correct algorithm selection is only the start of system design.

practice.question: Can a one-page coding example certify enterprise PQC security?
practice.answer: No; it omits protocol integration, validation, key management, access controls, and realistic testing.

lessons.misconception: Do not confuse QKD equipment with software-based PQC migration.

lessons.title: Role of the Quantum Technician
lessons.overview: Identify technician responsibilities and the evidence needed to operate, align, maintain, and troubleshoot quantum-adjacent equipment.

concepts.heading: The technician's place on a team
concepts.text: Technicians implement safe procedures, assemble and align instruments, gather repeatable measurements, record maintenance, and report anomalies. Engineers and scientists may define designs and models; the technician turns procedures into reliable evidence.

concepts.heading: Core practical skills
concepts.text: Typical skills include optical alignment, fiber handling, oscilloscope and function generator setup, power and signal monitoring, vacuum or cryogenic awareness when applicable, scripting, instrument documentation, calibration checks, and laboratory safety.

concepts.heading: Troubleshooting as a method
concepts.text: Start with a documented expected result, isolate the subsystem, verify the power/reference/settings/units, change one variable, capture data, then state what the results do and do not establish. Never bypass laser or electrical safety controls.

worked.title: Diagnose a missing interference trace
steps: Confirm that the oscilloscope and function generator are powered and share the expected reference.
Check the channel, coupling, probe factor, timebase, trigger, and amplitude settings.
Verify each input independently before combining signals.
Inspect wiring and connector continuity with outputs disabled.
Record the fault, correction, and a before/after waveform.
worked.result: A technician provides reproducible observations and a bounded diagnosis.

practice.question: Why is a screenshot without instrument settings insufficient?
practice.answer: Without scales, probe factors, offsets, and connections, another technician may not be able to interpret or reproduce it.

lessons.misconception: A technician does not have to prove quantum advantage to demonstrate excellent laboratory practice.

lessons.title: Python for Quantum
lessons.overview: Write a few safe, readable Python programs for complex amplitudes, normalization, and sampling—before using Qiskit.

concepts.heading: Why Python is helpful
concepts.text: Python is used to automate experiments, plot data, analyze counts, organize uncertainty, and build quantum circuits. Variables hold values, lists hold sequences, loops repeat tasks, and functions make calculations reusable.

concepts.heading: Complex amplitudes and probabilities
concepts.text: Python uses j for the imaginary unit: 1j. For a state with complex amplitudes a and b, compute abs(a)**2 and abs(b)**2, then verify that their sum is approximately 1. Floats have rounding error.

concepts.heading: From ideal probability to data
concepts.text: Use a reproducible random seed for classroom simulations; sample many shots; count 0s and 1s; calculate experimental frequencies and compare with ideal values. Simulated data are not real hardware measurements.

worked.title: Run a five-line state calculation
steps: from math import sqrt
a = 1 / sqrt(2)
b = 1j / sqrt(2)
p0, p1 = abs(a)**2, abs(b)**2
print(round(p0, 3), round(p1, 3))  # 0.5 0.5
worked.result: The amplitudes are complex; their squared magnitudes are real probabilities that sum to 1.

practice.question: Set a=3/5 and b=4j/5. What should Python print for probabilities?

lessons.misconception: The expression a*a is not generally a quantum probability when a is complex; use abs(a)**2.

lessons.title: Review of previous day
lessons.overview: Connect technician evidence records and Python calculations to the Saturday applied laboratory.

concepts.heading: Revisit the technician workflow
concepts.text: Predict, configure, measure, document, and report; isolate faults without losing records of the original setup.

concepts.heading: Revisit Python
concepts.text: Know why abs(a)**2 computes a complex amplitude's probability and why small floating-point errors are expected.

concepts.heading: Prepare for waves
concepts.text: Recall that frequency is the number of cycles each second and that relative phase describes how far one waveform is shifted from another.

worked.title: Predict before experimenting
steps: Set both ideal sine waves to the same frequency and amplitude.
Choose relative phase 0°: the signals reinforce.
Choose relative phase 180°: opposite signals cancel in a linear sum.
Record what would change if one source had different amplitude or frequency.
worked.result: The interference prediction is conditional on ideal equal-amplitude, coherent sources.

practice.question: Why change one setting at a time in a lab?
practice.answer: That helps identify cause and effect and reduces ambiguity when troubleshooting.

lessons.misconception: A physical scope trace has uncertainty and loading effects that an ideal graph does not.

lessons.title: Polarity and energy waves
lessons.overview: Distinguish electrical polarity, waveform amplitude, frequency, and phase, using clear sign conventions.

concepts.heading: Voltage polarity and reference
concepts.text: Voltage is a potential difference between two points. A positive measurement means the probe tip is at higher potential than the defined reference. Reversing the probes changes the voltage sign; it does not make the circuit's energy disappear.

concepts.heading: Wave vocabulary
concepts.text: A sine wave can be modeled as v(t)=A sin(2πft+φ). A is peak amplitude, f is frequency in hertz, and φ is phase. Period T=1/f. Peak-to-peak voltage is 2A for a zero-offset symmetric sine.

concepts.heading: Relative phase
concepts.text: Two equal-frequency waves can have different phase offsets. In an ideal linear sum they reinforce at 0° and cancel at 180° when amplitudes are equal and signs are consistent. Instrument ground clips must follow manufacturer safety rules.

worked.title: Read a waveform's numbers
steps: Suppose a sine wave has 2 V peak amplitude and frequency 1,000 Hz.
Its peak-to-peak voltage is 4 Vpp.
Its period is 1/1,000 s = 1 ms.
A quarter-cycle phase shift is 90°, corresponding to 0.25 ms at 1 kHz.
worked.result: Do not confuse 2 V peak with 2 Vpp; one is twice the other for this ideal sine.

practice.question: At 500 Hz, what is the period?

lessons.misconception: A minus sign depends on the chosen measurement reference; it is not automatically an unsafe condition.

lessons.title: Applied energy waves
lessons.overview: Perform a supervised classical interference demonstration with a function generator and oscilloscope, then calculate what the traces mean.

concepts.heading: Experimental setup
concepts.text: Use instructor-approved low-voltage sources, properly rated probes, and a common reference. For a two-output function generator, keep channels electrically separated with two equal resistors connected to a measurement node. Never tie active signal outputs together directly.

concepts.heading: What the circuit measures
concepts.text: For equal 10 kΩ resistors feeding a high-impedance input, the node voltage is approximately the average of two source voltages: vS=(vA+vB)/2. For matched sine amplitudes A, the ideal output peak amplitude is A|cos(φ/2)|, not twice A.

concepts.heading: Evidence and quantum analogy
concepts.text: At 0° the average amplitude is A; at 90° it is about 0.707A; at 180° ideally 0. The normalized squared amplitude cos²(φ/2) has the same mathematical dependence as one output of a simple ideal H–phase–H quantum circuit. A resistor/oscilloscope demo is classical; it does not generate qubits.

worked.title: Predict the output before measuring
steps: Set two synchronized sources to 1 kHz, 2 Vpp, and 0 V DC offset.
At 0° phase difference, predict node output 2.000 Vpp.
At 90°, predict 2 × cos45° ≈ 1.414 Vpp.
At 180°, predict nearly 0.000 Vpp.
Record measured values, instrument scaling, resistor values, and percent differences.
worked.result: Compare ideal theory to real measured voltage and report instrument limitations.

practice.question: A student sees 0.1 Vpp at 180°. Does the model necessarily fail?
practice.answer: No. Source mismatch, phase error, finite loading, probe settings, and measurement uncertainty can leave a residual signal.

lessons.misconception: Never connect a grounded oscilloscope probe clip to a non-ground live node or assume channels are isolated.

lessons.title: Future Projects
lessons.overview: Turn workshop concepts into scoped projects with a measurable result and a realistic resource plan.

concepts.heading: Choose an achievable question
concepts.text: Useful beginner projects include a Bloch-sphere gate visualizer, BB84 basis-sifting simulator, Qiskit Bell-state notebook, Python photon-count histogram, polarization experiment, or automated low-voltage oscilloscope record. Start with one question and a clearly identified model.

concepts.heading: Plan equipment and permissions
concepts.text: List what you already have, what needs instructor supervision, and which systems require an authorized account. Never claim laboratory access, a certificate, or measured hardware results without evidence.

concepts.heading: Define milestones and proof
concepts.text: Specify an objective, theory/prediction, materials/software, safety constraints, demonstration, measured or simulated data, limitations, and a concise presentation. Use a short checklist so another student can reproduce your outcome.

worked.title: Example project pitch
steps: Question: How does relative phase change the outcome of an ideal H–P(φ)–H circuit?
Build a small Python model for φ=0°, 90°, and 180°.
Predict P(0)=cos²(φ/2): 1, 0.5, and 0.
Compare with the portal's classical interference model, making clear what is analogy and what is quantum model.
Submit a graph, equations, code, and limitations.
worked.result: One well-tested, reproducible demonstration is stronger than several unverified claims.

practice.question: What proves a project is ready to demonstrate?
practice.answer: A reproducible procedure, clear expected/observed results, safety review, and honest statement of limitations.

lessons.misconception: The source agenda does not specify a time or presenter for Future Projects; this is supplemental planning material.
